content: The logic model for nutrition interventions can be adapted and applied to wheat flour fortification programs. Member States have the flexibility to modify this model and use it alongside appropriate indicators to design, implement, monitor, and evaluate the success of nutrition actions within public health programs. The WHO/CDC eCatalogue of indicators for micronutrient programs and the manual for flour fortification utilize this logic model, which can be tailored for programs aimed at fortifying wheat flour with essential vitamins and minerals. The typical nutritional value for fortified blended foods, including Corn-Soy Blend (CSB), as per the World Food Programme, includes a minimum of 380 kcal of energy, 18% protein, 6% fat, and a range of micronutrients such as vitamins A, B6, B12, C, D, E, K, calcium, folic acid, zinc, iron, niacin, pantothenic acid, potassium, riboflavin, and thiamine. The WHO eCatalogue is a user-friendly web resource designed for professionals involved in providing technical assistance in monitoring, evaluation, and surveillance of public health programs implementing micronutrient interventions. It offers potential indicators with standardized definitions that can be selected, downloaded, and adapted to local program contexts. Since 1991, WHO has maintained the Micronutrients Database as part of the Vitamin and Mineral Nutrition Information System (VMNIS). This database supports WHO’s mandate to assess the micronutrient status of populations, monitor and evaluate the impact of strategies to prevent and control micronutrient malnutrition, and track related trends over time. The VMNIS Micronutrient Database is managed by the WHO Department of Nutrition and Food Safety in collaboration with regional and country offices and national health authorities. At the global level, WHO has developed a web-based Global Targets Tracking Tool, which allows users to explore scenarios to achieve the progress rates required to meet the 2025 global nutrition targets, including a 50% reduction in anemia among women of reproductive age. This platform also serves as a centralized resource for sharing information on nutrition actions implemented worldwide, providing examples of how guidelines are translated into practice. The Global Database on the Implementation of Nutrition Actions (GINA) offers valuable information on the implementation of various nutrition policies and interventions. Since its launch in November 2012, the use of GINA has steadily increased. The development of this guideline followed WHO’s evidence-informed guideline development procedures, as outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. The process began in February 2010 and included the creation of guidelines for fortifying five staple foods (wheat, maize, rice, condiments, sugar, and oil) with key micronutrients such as iron, folates, vitamin A, zinc, and iodine. These nutrients are critical for health and development, and their deficiencies can have severe consequences at both individual and public health levels. A WHO steering committee, led by the Department of Nutrition and Food Safety, was established to oversee the guideline development process. Two additional groups were formed: a guideline development group and a systematic reviews team. The guideline development group included experts from various WHO expert advisory panels and specialists identified through open calls, ensuring a balanced gender mix, multidisciplinary expertise, and representation from all WHO regions. The systematic reviews team conducted Cochrane systematic reviews to evaluate the benefits and harms of wheat flour fortification with vitamins and minerals (iron, folic acid, zinc, or vitamin A) on micronutrient status and health-related outcomes in the general population. Evidence summaries were prepared using the GRADE approach to assess the overall certainty of the evidence. The final draft guideline underwent peer review by four content experts who provided technical feedback. These reviewers were not involved in the guideline development process but were tasked with identifying errors, missing data, and issues related to clarity and implementation. The guideline development process included the management of competing interests. All experts participating in WHO meetings were required to declare any relevant interests before their participation. These declarations were reviewed by the responsible technical officer and relevant departments to ensure transparency and objectivity. The guideline development group used the PICO (Population, Intervention, Control, Outcomes) format to frame key questions and identify critical outcomes for decision-making. These questions were reviewed and modified as needed by the steering committee and guideline development group. The guideline builds on previous work, including technical workshops and systematic reviews of evidence on wheat flour fortification. WHO commissioned Cochrane systematic reviews to determine the efficacy and effectiveness of fortification programs, as well as the forms and levels of fortificants currently used in different countries. The final recommendations were developed through a consensus-building process within the guideline development group. If unanimous agreement was not reached, additional deliberations and online voting were conducted. A two-thirds majority vote was required for approval of the recommendations if consensus could not be achieved. This document represents WHO’s official guideline and reflects the organization’s decisions, policies, and views. It provides a comprehensive framework for fortifying wheat flour with vitamins and minerals as a public health strategy, ensuring evidence-based and transparent decision-making processes.
